issues.legal_issue: A common object under the unlawful-assembly provision may arise after people have assembled for a lawful purpose, without prior concert, if five or more people come to share an unlawful object and act together to achieve it.
material_facts: People gathered in response to cries and the noise of a fight, so the gathering did not initially establish an unlawful purpose.
The accepted evidence showed that the accused joined in beating the injured people and those who came to assist them.
The fact-finding courts concluded that five or more of the accused shared an unlawful object to beat the victims and acted together.
issues.conclusion: The findings supported convictions for rioting and causing hurt as members of an unlawful assembly; prior consultation or a prior meeting of minds was not necessary.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 149 and 34 of the Indian Penal Code, common object and common intention are distinct concepts. Section 149 requires an assembly of five or more sharing an unlawful object, but does not require prior concert or a prior meeting of minds. An initially lawful object may develop into an unlawful one; mere presence at the gathering is not enough, and the court must determine who shared and acted on the unlawful object. No earlier case is cited for this principle.

predicates.unlawful_assembly_conviction_challenge: The proceeding challenges a conviction based on participation in an unlawful assembly.
predicates.five_or_more_shared_unlawful_object: Five or more people came to share the same unlawful purpose, whether before or after assembling.
predicates.acted_together_to_achieve_object: The people sharing that purpose acted together to carry it out.

issues.definition: When an unlawful-assembly conviction is challenged, the rule supports liability if at least five people shared an unlawful purpose and acted together to achieve it, even if that purpose formed after they assembled.

issues.legal_issue: A participant in an unlawful assembly may be liable for a killing committed in pursuit of its common object when the killing was a likely consequence of the assault and the participant knew that it was likely.
material_facts: The assault involved firearms and other weapons, and people joined in beating victims who had already been shot or knocked to the ground.
Several people participated in the beating, and four victims died.
The court concluded that a person of reasonable intelligence would have known that death was likely in a melee of this kind.
issues.conclusion: The convictions for murder through the unlawful-assembly provision could be upheld because the killing was a likely consequence of the assault and the participants knew that it was likely.
issues.legal_principle: For liability under section 149 of the Indian Penal Code for a killing beyond the common object to beat, the court required both that a killing was likely to result from the beating forming the common object and that each person convicted knew it might be a likely result. No earlier case is cited for this principle.

rule.if: common_object_homicide_appeal and assault_resulted_in_death and death_was_likely_from_assault and participant_knew_death_was_likely

predicates.common_object_homicide_appeal: The proceeding challenges liability for a homicide attributed to members of a group sharing a common object.
predicates.assault_resulted_in_death: The collective assault resulted in one or more deaths.
predicates.death_was_likely_from_assault: The nature and circumstances of the assault made a death a likely consequence.
predicates.participant_knew_death_was_likely: The participant knew that a death was likely to result from the assault.

issues.definition: The rule makes a participant liable for a killing when, in a challenge to group liability for homicide, the group assault caused death, death was a likely consequence, and the participant knew it was likely.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court does not ordinarily reappraise evidence in a special-leave criminal appeal to displace concurrent factual findings merely because fact-finders accepted part of a witness’s testimony and rejected another part.
material_facts: The fact-finding courts made concurrent findings based on the portions of witness testimony they accepted.
The appellants argued that testimony was unsafe to rely on because other portions of the same witnesses’ evidence had been rejected.
The challenge asked the Supreme Court to review the evidence in a special-leave appeal.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court declined to review the concurrent findings or reappraise the evidence.
issues.legal_principle: In exercising its jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Court followed its practice of not reviewing concurrent factual findings merely because a fact-finder accepted one part of a witness’s evidence and rejected another. No earlier case is named in the judgment for this point.

predicates.special_leave_criminal_appeal: The proceeding is a criminal appeal brought by special leave.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings: The lower fact-finding courts reached the same factual findings.
predicates.challenge_seeks_evidentiary_reappraisal: The appellant asks the Supreme Court to revisit the evidence underlying those findings.

issues.definition: In a special-leave criminal appeal, the Supreme Court does not reappraise evidence when the lower courts made concurrent factual findings and the challenge seeks their reconsideration.

issues.legal_issue: A claim that a defect in the charge caused prejudice may be declined when the claim lacks particulars and the objection was not raised at an early stage.
material_facts: The appellants claimed that an omission in the charge caused prejudice but supplied no particulars of prejudice in their leave petitions.
The objection had not been raised at an early stage.
The appellants’ only specific complaint about prejudice concerned the examination under section 342 of the Criminal Procedure Code, and the Court declined to allow the matter to be raised.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to entertain the prejudice objection.
issues.legal_principle: The Court stated that it would be slow to entertain a claim of prejudice when details were not furnished and would take into account whether the objection was raised at an early stage. No earlier case is named in the judgment for this principle.

predicates.criminal_appeal_prejudice_challenge: The proceeding includes a criminal appellant’s claim that a procedural defect caused prejudice.
predicates.no_particulars_of_prejudice: The appellant does not provide details showing how the alleged defect caused prejudice.
predicates.objection_not_raised_early: The appellant did not raise the objection at an early stage of the proceeding.

issues.definition: A prejudice claim in a criminal appeal is not entertained when the appellant provides no particulars of prejudice and did not raise the objection early.
